records.sourceFile: Heads Up for creatine supplementation and its potential applications for brain health and function.pdf

paper.citation: Candow DG, Forbes SC, Ostojic SM, Prokopidis K, Stock MS, Harmon KK, et al. "Heads Up" for Creatine Supplementation and its Potential Applications for Brain Health and Function. Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarizes research on creatine supplementation and brain health and function, and discusses possible sex and age differences in response. The authors report that creatine can increase brain creatine stores, which may explain some benefits for cognition and memory, especially in aging adults or during metabolic stress such as sleep deprivation. They also describe promise for TBI (including concussion in children), muscular dystrophy, depression and anxiety, while noting that sex and age differences are largely unknown.
paper.tldr: Creatine may support cognition under stress such as sleep deprivation and may help some brain conditions, but most of the evidence is from animals, older adults or patients. Brain creatine rises only with high doses (about 20 g per day) over weeks, and athlete data are very limited.
paper.methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy, inclusion criteria or quality appraisal. Sections cover brain bioenergetics, cognitive function, TBI, neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis, ALS, muscular dystrophies, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease) and mood disorders, drawing on animal and human studies. The paper is based on a presentation to the Gatorade Sports Science Institute Expert Panel.
paper.findings: The authors cite evidence that high-dose creatine (about 20 g per day or more) is needed over several weeks to raise brain creatine, for example an 8.7% rise in total brain creatine after 20 g per day for 4 weeks in 9 healthy people. Human cognitive results are mixed; benefits appear more often under sleep deprivation, hypoxia or mental fatigue, including attenuated loss of passing accuracy in 10 sleep-deprived elite male rugby players given 50 or 100 mg/kg before testing. For TBI, animal studies show reduced cortical damage, and an open-label trial in 39 children and adolescents (0.4 g/kg/day for 6 months) reported shorter post-traumatic amnesia and better recovery; trials in Parkinson's disease and ALS were largely negative.
paper.limitations: The review gives no search or selection method, so the evidence summarized may be selective. Much of the evidence is from rodents or patient populations, sex-specific responses come mainly from animal models, and the pediatric TBI trial was open-label with no sex-based analysis. The authors declare creatine-industry relationships and the supplement was funded by GSSI, a division of PepsiCo.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners should not expect standard muscle-loading doses to change brain creatine, since the review cites about 20 g per day for several weeks as needed. Creatine's possible cognitive benefit during sleep loss is supported by a few small studies, including one in rugby players, and should be presented as preliminary. The review does not support creatine as a concussion treatment for athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Evidence that creatine protects skill or cognitive performance during sleep deprivation comes from a few small trials, including one in 10 elite male rugby players. It is not enough to set doses or expected effects for athletes.
paper.rtp: The review cannot inform return-to-play decisions after concussion. The human TBI evidence is one open-label pediatric trial in hospital TBI patients, and the authors call for more research before conclusions are drawn.

records.sourceFile: High prevalence of prior contact sports play and concussion among orthopedic and neurosurgical department chairs.pdf

paper.citation: Sone JY, Lamb SCK, Techar K, Dammavalam V, Uppal M, Williams C, et al. High prevalence of prior contact sports play and concussion among orthopedic and neurosurgical department chairs. J Neurosurg Pediatr. 2018.
paper.abstract: This survey compared high school and college contact sport participation and lifetime concussion history among US orthopedic and neurosurgery department chairs with historical population norms. Chairs reported much higher rates of contact sport and football play and of at least one concussion (about 42%) than the general population. The authors conclude that individuals in careers requiring high motor and cognitive function frequently played contact sports, and call for study of both long-term benefits and risks.
paper.tldr: Surgical department chairs reported playing youth contact sports and having concussions far more often than historical population norms. The study shows these histories did not preclude high-level surgical careers, not that contact sport or concussion is harmless.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional email survey of 107 orthopedic and 74 neurosurgery department chairs at ACGME-accredited US programs, asking about high school and college contact sport play (American Academy of Pediatrics definition) and lifetime concussion. Responses were compared with male norms derived from 1970 to 1980 high school and 1981 to 1990 NCAA and census data and a 12% concussion prevalence, using one-proportion Z-tests, chi-square tests and binary logistic regression. Analyses were repeated assuming all nonrespondents had not played contact sport or had no concussion.
paper.findings: High school contact sport play was 65.3% (orthopedic) and 47.9% (neurosurgery) against a 27.74% norm, and high school football 46.9% and 33.3% against 10.91%; college contact sport was 44.7% and 21.7% against 1.44%, and college football 21.3% and 6.5% against 0.758%. At least one lifetime concussion was reported by 42.6% and 42.4% of chairs against a 12% norm, and most chairs who described a cause attributed it to contact sports, mainly football. High school contact sport play was associated with higher odds of prior concussion after adjusting for specialty (OR 10.6, 95% CI 3.7 to 30.8).
paper.limitations: Self-report and recall bias, moderate response rates (about 44 to 65%) and possible response bias toward sport-interested chairs; the authors also note physicians may recognize concussion more readily than laypeople. There were no standard definitions of sport participation or concussion, the 12% norm is a general adult TBI prevalence, norms were male-only and era-specific, and only one respondent was female. The worst-case model gives a much larger odds ratio (35.5) because nonrespondents were coded as having neither exposure nor concussion.
paper.practicalImplications: The findings can inform discussion that youth contact sport participation does not by itself preclude later high-level cognitive and motor careers. They do not show benefit from contact sport, and the authors stress that the risks of head impacts and their sequelae cannot be dismissed. High school contact sport play was associated with a much higher self-reported lifetime concussion rate in this group.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable to training or performance. The study describes past sport participation and career attainment in surgeons.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform concussion management or return-to-play decisions. It measured self-reported concussion history only, with no injury details, recovery data or clinical outcomes.
